title: Virtues grow (CCC 1804)
hook: virtues are habits built by repeated good acts

segments.voice: Yesterday, forming conscience: a voice to obey, and a voice to teach. Your line was an educated conscience.

How does someone become honest? Not by one brave decision on a Monday morning. Watch a baker's apprentice in her first week. The dough sticks to the counter, to her fingers, to her sleeves. The loaves come out flat. Every fold takes thought, and most go wrong. Then another morning, and another, and without anyone marking the moment, something changes. A year on, the same hands fold the dough while she talks about the weather. Nobody gave her that skill in one go. She built it, one sticky morning at a time, until her hands knew before her head did.
screen: `HOW DOES SOMEONE BECOME HONEST?` → `ONE STICKY MORNING AT A TIME.` → `HER HANDS JUST KNOW.`

segments.voice: Back on day three hundred fourteen, you met the four hinges, the cardinal virtues. Today, how virtue grows. The Catechism defines virtue simply: a habitual and firm disposition to do the good. Not one good deed, but a settled way of being, so good acts come more readily. It describes the human virtues as firm attitudes, stable dispositions, habitual perfections of intellect and will. They govern our actions, order our passions, and guide our conduct by reason and faith. Notice the middle one: they order the passions. That picks up two days ago: feelings aren't sins, but they need a shape, and virtue gives them one. And virtue makes possible ease, self-mastery and joy in living a good life. Ease, like the baker who no longer thinks about her hands. The honest person stops arguing with themselves every time a lie would be easier. The virtuous person, the Catechism says, freely practices the good. Then the line behind today's title: these virtues are acquired by human effort. They are the fruit and the seed of morally good acts. Fruit, because good acts repeated build the habit. Seed, because the habit makes the next good act more likely. A circle that turns toward the good. Saint Paul, quoted by the Catechism just before, tells the Philippians to think on whatever is true, just, holy and lovely, if there be any virtue. Think on these things, he says. Then, do them.
screen: `A FIRM HABIT OF DOING GOOD.` · `IT GIVES THE PASSIONS A SHAPE.` · `EASE, SELF-MASTERY AND JOY.` · `THE FRUIT AND THE SEED OF GOOD ACTS.`

segments.voice: Pick one small good thing you did recently that cost you a little, holding your tongue, writing back kindly, washing someone else's cup, and picture yourself doing it again, in the same ordinary way. Don't aim for something heroic; aim for something you could do a hundred times. If you pray, ask for help to keep at it; if you don't, just decide where and when.
Virtue. A firm habit of doing good, built by repeated good acts: the fruit of those acts, and the seed of the next ones. Today's word.
Your line: habits of good. Each good act makes the next one a little easier. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching describes the human virtues as habits acquired by education, deliberate good acts and perseverance, and Catholics work on them through daily practice, the examination of conscience and the sacraments.

chat.says: How do people actually become more patient? Is it just something you're born with?
options: The Catechism says virtues are acquired by human effort: good acts, repeated, until they come readily.
Yes. Virtues are fixed at birth, so if you aren't patient now, practice won't really change it.
No. One big, dramatic act of patience is enough to make you a patient person for good.
chat.meaning: The Catechism calls virtue a firm habit of doing good, acquired by human effort. Good acts are its fruit and its seed, so each one makes the next more likely.
